fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: Multiplex immunofluorescence measures selected protein-marker signals in a tissue section, using one or several imaging cycles. Cyclic methods build a high-plex image of one section by repeating staining, imaging and signal removal and then registering the cycles: t-CyCIF produced up to 60-plex images of formalin-fixed specimens and showed that antigenicity changes with cycle number (Lin and colleagues, 2018), and IBEX imaged more than 65 parameters in one section by iterative staining and chemical bleaching (Radtke and colleagues, 2020). A six-institution study of a six-plex PD-1 and PD-L1 panel, imaged with a locked-down image analysis algorithm, reported average intersite concordance of cell densities of R squared 0.75 in breast carcinoma and 0.72 in non-small cell lung cancer tissue microarrays (Taube and colleagues, 2021); that is reproducibility for one specified panel and workflow, not for multiplex immunofluorescence in general. A cell phenotype is a rule-based call from the measured panel, a density needs a stated denominator, and a distance needs a stated definition (cell centre or cell boundary).

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: The original imaging mass cytometry method combined metal-tagged antibodies with laser ablation and mass cytometry to map marker signals in tumor sections. Multiplexed ion beam imaging is a related approach that uses secondary ion mass spectrometry; the acquisition methods are distinct. Assigning tissue signals to individual cells also requires image analysis. Marker selection, antibody performance and segmentation affect what a reported cell profile means; a spatial association does not by itself establish a cellular mechanism or treatment response. The original imaging mass cytometry paper coupled immunohistochemical and immunocytochemical staining with high-resolution laser ablation to CyTOF mass cytometry, imaging 32 proteins and modifications at subcellular resolution in human breast cancer samples, with more than 100 markers possible given further isotopes; mass cytometry had previously been applied only to cell suspensions (Giesen and colleagues, 2014). Spillover between channels is reduced compared with dye-based flow cytometry but still exists, and a bead-based compensation workflow was developed to estimate and correct it in suspension and imaging mass cytometry, reducing the risk of reporting cell phenotype artefacts (Chevrier and colleagues, 2018).

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: Reading guide (OnCo inference built on the sources). Bottom-up proteomics digests proteins to peptides, separates them by liquid chromatography, measures ions and fragments by tandem mass spectrometry, and identifies peptides by software, so evidence for an intact, functional protein is indirect. A shared peptide cannot choose between candidate proteins; inference uses the other peptides recovered and reports ambiguity. A ratio needs its denominator, an absolute amount needs calibration with standards in a matched matrix (Carr and colleagues, 2014), and a peptide standard does not by itself show recovery of the original protein. A bulk extract mixes cells and loses their positions, so a peptide signal per mass of extract is not receptors per cancer cell.

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: Reading guide (OnCo inference). Kinases add phosphate and phosphatases remove it, as the existing phosphorylation record states, and a larger phosphopeptide signal is not a universal sign of greater activity. Enrichment changes what is recovered, so a phosphopeptide sample is not an unbiased count of all proteins. Site localisation is separate from peptide identification and carries its own confidence. A phosphopeptide intensity reflects the source-protein amount, the modified fraction and recovery, so intensity or fold change is not occupancy. A set of supported sites can inform a pathway hypothesis; it does not measure the pathway's rate, prove dependence or show benefit from a drug, and a kinase inferred from a pattern is not measured causality.

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: Fictional worked example with independent arithmetic. Parent-protein signal rises from 100 to 200 and phosphopeptide signal from 20 to 40, each on its own assay scale: 200 / 100 = 2 and 40 / 20 = 2, so the protein-adjusted relative change is 2 / 2 = 1. The raw 20 / 100 = 0.2 is not the fraction of protein molecules carrying the site, because recovery and response factors differ between the assays, and no activation or kinase-causality conclusion follows. A twofold phosphopeptide rise with a twofold parent-protein rise therefore does not show doubled activation.

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: Mass-spectrometry and antibody-based methods measure different protein-derived signals under defined workflows. A primary yeast study measured protein expression alongside phosphorylation and showed why a changed phosphopeptide signal can reflect protein abundance as well as phosphorylation. That methodological result is not a validated cancer-treatment rule. Targeted plasma-protein assays likewise require evidence about recovery, calibration and quantitative range. A protein measurement, modification-site signal, functional pathway dependence and prediction of treatment benefit are distinct claims. Beausoleil and colleagues introduced the Ascore, a probability-based score for how likely a phosphorylation site is correctly localised from site-determining ions in tandem mass spectra, alongside a target-decoy measure of dataset error (2006). In yeast, 25 per cent of seemingly differential phosphopeptides were attributable to changes in protein expression once phosphopeptide ratios were calibrated by protein levels (Wu and colleagues, 2011). In human ovarian tumour and breast cancer xenograft tissue collected without vascular interruption, rapid phosphorylation changes were seen in up to 24 per cent of the phosphoproteome after defined ischaemic intervals, while the global proteome and most of more than 25,000 quantified phosphosites were unchanged after 60 minutes; phosphopeptides in that study were enriched by immobilised metal (Fe3+) affinity chromatography before analysis (Mertins and colleagues, 2014).

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: Reading guide (OnCo inference built on the ICH definitions). A signal detected below the quantification limit is meaningful as detection, but it does not support a reliable amount, and neither it nor non-detection means biological zero. An upper limit also bounds the range, and a saturated response cannot separate larger inputs. Keep the denominator with every amount (for example femtomoles per microgram of total extracted protein or a concentration per volume), because it describes the mixture and not receptors per malignant cell; a selected peptide is a proxy for its source protein and cannot count intact receptors or surface copies. Tight repeats show precision, which can coexist with systematic bias. A standard added after digestion can control later measurement but cannot correct material already lost.

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: A primary multilaboratory study evaluated isotope-dilution multiple-reaction-monitoring assays for selected plasma proteins, examining recovery, reproducibility, linear range, detection and quantification limits. The performance belonged to the tested materials, analytes and protocols. It was not a universal certificate for all proteins or specimens. A reported protein amount should retain its measured peptide, calibration approach, sample preparation and supported range. An NIH workshop report on targeted mass spectrometry found no consensus on the criteria for a successful peptide assay and set out three tiers of assay performance, with response and calibration curves generated for each analyte in the relevant matrix to establish limits of detection and quantification; quantification rests on precursor-product ion pairs, called transitions, shown to be free of interference, and a surrogate protein standard must be shown to behave like the native analyte in tests of recovery after adding a known amount (Carr and colleagues, 2014). Stable-isotope-labelled internal standard peptides with the sequence of the analyte are spiked into the digest, and extended peptides or recombinant proteins can compensate for variability in digestion (Hoofnagle and colleagues, 2016). A multilaboratory plasma study reported reproducibility, recovery, linear range and limits of detection and quantification at microgram-per-millilitre protein concentrations (Addona and colleagues, 2009).

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: Reading guide (definitions plus OnCo inference). Detection asks whether a cell was found, segmentation asks which pixels belong to it, and phenotyping classifies the cell afterwards; finding a nucleus does not give a reliable whole-cell boundary. Intersection over union is the area two masks share divided by the area either covers, from 0 to 1, and a single value can hide missed or merged cells, so check object counts and characteristic errors too. A mask assigns existing signals to estimated regions and is not a measurement of a new marker. Merging, splitting and missing cells distort counts, marker combinations and spatial relations, so overlay masks on the original channels.

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: The Mesmer study developed and tested whole-cell segmentation across tissue images and used the estimated boundaries to extract cellular features. A separate spatial-transcriptomics reanalysis found that misassigned molecules could change downstream cell-state and interaction analyses. These findings concern defined datasets and methods, not one universal error rate. Segmentation quality and signal assignment need evaluation before a spatial measurement is treated as a biological conclusion. Mesmer was trained on TissueNet, a dataset of more than 1 million manually labelled cells, and was reported to generalise across the tissue types and imaging platforms in that dataset at human-level performance; its authors note that segmentation inaccuracies can substantially bias the identification and counting of cells, and that cells whose nucleus lies outside the imaging plane are missed by nucleus-based methods (Greenwald and colleagues, 2022). In that evaluation, a predicted and a true cell with a one-to-one match by intersection over union count as accurate, predicted cells with no match are false positives and true cells with no match are false negatives. The Cellpose study reported a generalist method trained on more than 70,000 segmented objects that worked without retraining across the image types it evaluated (Stringer and colleagues, 2021). Baysor was developed because methods that approximate cell positions from nuclear stains make cell boundaries hard to distinguish in single-molecule spatial data (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022).

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: A reverse-phase protein array places sample lysates on an array and measures selected proteins or modifications with antibodies. The original tissue study examined signaling proteins in defined cell populations. A later study used phosphatase treatment as an independent control when characterizing phospho-antibodies for frozen and fixed tissue. Signal specificity, input preparation and validation matter. A lysate measurement does not restore the spatial arrangement lost during extraction, and phosphorylation signal needs interpretation alongside protein abundance. In the original reverse-phase protein microarray, the whole repertoire of a patient's tissue proteins from laser-capture microdissected cell populations is immobilised and probed, in contrast to earlier arrays that immobilise the probe, and precision and linearity were tested with microarrayed dilution curves of a standard protein and loading was normalised with an actin control (Paweletz and colleagues, 2001). Because target detection relies on a single antibody, RNA interference was used to test antibody performance: two anti-EGFR antibodies detected knockdown at different rates, and four of ten anti-STAT3 antibodies detected STAT3 knockdown at 80 to 85 per cent (Mannsperger and colleagues, 2010). Ischaemia changed phosphorylation in human ovarian tumour tissue and breast cancer xenografts, which supports recording how tissue was collected and preserved without setting a universal safe delay (Mertins and colleagues, 2014).

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: The limit of blank describes an upper background response at a specified probability. A limit of detection concerns an amount that can be detected under stated false-call and detection-probability conditions; LoD95 specifies 95 per cent detection in the tested workflow. It is not a line above which every repeat must be positive, nor 95 per cent certainty that a person has disease. A limit of quantitation requires stated quantitative accuracy, including bias and imprecision goals. The limits answer different questions and have no universal spacing; they may coincide under a particular method and its criteria.

fieldProofs.supportingExcerpt: Fictional assay example: the blank-response axis describes background readings, while a separate known-input axis has LoD95 at 2 units.
